cards.statement: An implementing class inherits static methods declared by its interfaces.
cards.explanation: An interface's static methods belong to that interface; a class implementation inherits none of them.
cards.misconception: Interface static methods become inherited class members.

cards.statement: An inherited public instance method with a body wins over a matching interface default method.
cards.explanation: A concrete instance method inherited from a superclass supplies the implementation instead of the matching interface default.

cards.statement: A class resolves conflicting interface defaults using the order of its implements clause.
cards.explanation: Matching defaults from unrelated interfaces create a compile-time conflict. The class resolves it by overriding the method.
cards.misconception: The order of implemented interfaces determines which conflicting default wins.

cards.statement: An interface accepts `default String toString() { return "x"; }`.
cards.explanation: An interface's default toString implementation produces a compile-time error because it matches a non-private Object method.
cards.misconception: An interface default can provide an implementation of Object.toString.

cards.statement: An interface field declaration such as `int LIMIT = 10;` declares a public static final field.
cards.explanation: Java supplies public, static and final for interface fields when their declarations omit those modifiers.

cards.statement: An enum declaration accepts a protected constructor.
cards.explanation: Java rejects protected enum constructors at compile time. Enum constructors use private access, explicitly or implicitly.
cards.misconception: Enum constructors support protected access like ordinary class constructors.

cards.statement: An enum with a constant-specific class body is implicitly sealed.
cards.explanation: An enum constant's class body declares an anonymous subclass; those subclasses form the enum's permitted set.

cards.statement: `Status.values()` returns the constants of enum Status in their declaration order.
cards.explanation: The compiler supplies values() for an enum. Its returned array follows the order of the constants in the enum declaration.

cards.statement: `record Point(int x) {}` supplies a public accessor named `x()`.
cards.explanation: A record's generated accessor uses its component's name as the method name and returns that component's value.

source.title: Record Classes – Java SE 25 Language Guide

cards.statement: A compact record constructor assigns component fields after its body finishes normally.
cards.explanation: The compiler uses the component parameters' resulting values to initialize the fields after a compact constructor's body.

cards.statement: `record Box(List<String> items) {}` copies the supplied list in its generated canonical constructor.
cards.explanation: The generated Box constructor stores the supplied list reference. Copying a mutable component requires an explicit constructor implementation.
cards.misconception: A generated canonical record constructor makes defensive copies of mutable arguments.

cards.statement: Generated equals for `record Data(int[] values) {}` compares the array elements.
cards.explanation: The generated Data.equals method compares its values components by reference. Equal array contents alone do not make two Data records equal.
cards.misconception: Generated record equality compares an array component's contents.

cards.statement: A direct subclass of a sealed class requires one of `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.
cards.explanation: A direct subclass has one of these modifiers explicitly or implicitly. Its status controls whether developers can extend its branch.

cards.statement: In the unnamed module, a sealed class and its permitted direct subclasses may occupy different packages.
cards.explanation: In the unnamed module, a permitted direct subclass belongs to the same package as its sealed superclass.
cards.misconception: Sealed types in the unnamed module use the same cross-package rules as types in a named module.

cards.statement: A sealed class may infer its permitted direct subclasses from declarations in the same compilation unit.
cards.explanation: When a sealed class omits a permits clause, Java infers eligible direct subclasses declared in that compilation unit.

cards.statement: In a void method with `Object o`, `s` is in scope after `if (!(o instanceof String s)) return;`.
cards.explanation: A guard that returns when an instanceof String pattern fails leaves its binding variable in scope for the following statements.

cards.statement: With `record Box(Object x) {}`, `new Box(new Box("x"))` matches `Box(Box(String s))`.
cards.explanation: Nested record patterns match component values recursively. The outer Box holds a Box whose component is a String, so the pattern binds s to "x".

cards.statement: A switch statement with arrow labels continues into the next arm after the chosen arm completes.
cards.explanation: An arrow-label switch executes the selected arm and then exits the switch when that arm completes normally.
cards.misconception: Arrow-label switch statements preserve the fall-through behavior of colon labels.

cards.statement: For an int selector `x`, `switch (x) { default -> { yield 7; } }` evaluates to 7.
cards.explanation: Inside a switch expression, yield transfers a value out of the chosen block. A block that executes yield 7; produces the int value 7.

source.title: JLS 25 §15.28.2: Run-Time Evaluation of switch Expressions

cards.statement: `case String s` is a valid label after an unguarded `case CharSequence cs` in the same switch.
cards.explanation: The compiler rejects a String pattern after an unguarded CharSequence pattern because the preceding pattern already covers its matching values.
cards.misconception: A later, more specific pattern remains valid after an earlier pattern that already covers its values.

cards.statement: An enum switch statement with just enum-constant arrow cases requires exhaustiveness to pass compilation.
cards.explanation: An enum switch statement with just constant labels can omit constants. An omitted constant makes the statement complete normally without executing an arm.
cards.misconception: Arrow labels make an enum switch statement enhanced and therefore subject to exhaustive coverage.

source.title: JLS 25 §14.11.2: The Switch Block of a switch Statement

cards.statement: A switch expression can cover a sealed interface exhaustively using its permitted-subtype type patterns.
cards.explanation: Type-pattern cases covering a sealed selector's permitted subtypes provide exhaustive type coverage, so a default label is optional.

cards.statement: For `String s = null;`, `switch (s) { default -> {} }` completes normally.
cards.explanation: For a null String selector, a switch with a plain default label throws NullPointerException. That label does not match null.
cards.misconception: A default label handles a null selector along with other unmatched selector values.

cards.statement: Since Java 22, a later expression can read the value of `String _ = "x";` by using `_`.
cards.explanation: The underscore declares an unnamed variable but does not name it. An expression that tries to read that variable through _ is a compile-time error.
cards.misconception: An underscore declaration provides a placeholder name that later expressions can read.

cards.statement: A variable declared as `List<int>` holds a list parameterized with primitive int.
cards.explanation: Java rejects List<int> at compile time because a concrete generic type argument is a reference type.
cards.misconception: Java accepts primitive types as generic type arguments.

source.title: JLS SE 25 §4.5.1: Type Arguments of Parameterized Types

cards.statement: In `List<String> xs = new ArrayList<>();`, Java infers String for `<>`.
cards.explanation: The assignment target supplies String as ArrayList's inferred type argument, so the diamond creates an ArrayList<String>.

source.title: JLS SE 25 §15.9: Class Instance Creation Expressions

cards.statement: A `List<Integer>` reference fits a parameter declared as `List<Number>`.
cards.explanation: Java rejects passing List<Integer> as List<Number>. A subtype relationship between element classes does not transfer to these parameterized types.
cards.misconception: Generic containers inherit the subtype relationships of their element types.

source.title: JLS SE 25 §4.10.2: Subtyping among Class and Interface Types

cards.statement: With `Number[] xs = new Integer[1];`, `xs[0] = 1.5` throws ArrayStoreException.
cards.explanation: The array's actual component type is Integer. The Double value from 1.5 fails the run-time array store check.

cards.statement: Assigning a raw `List` to `List<String>` produces an unchecked warning.
cards.explanation: The unchecked conversion means the compiler cannot verify that the raw list contains String values.

cards.statement: The expression `new T()` compiles when `T` is a class type parameter.
cards.explanation: Java rejects new T() at compile time. A type parameter identifies an unknown type rather than a class whose constructor the expression can invoke.
cards.misconception: Java resolves a type parameter's no-argument constructor for new T().

source.title: JLS SE 25 §15.9.1: Determining the Class being Instantiated

cards.statement: Java creates an array of parameterized lists with `new List<String>[10]`.
cards.explanation: Java rejects new List<String>[10] at compile time because array creation requires a component type available for run-time checking.
cards.misconception: Java allows direct creation of arrays whose component types use concrete generic arguments.

cards.statement: Java treats `m(List<String>)` and `m(List<Integer>)` as distinct overloads in one class.
cards.explanation: Both method declarations erase to m(List), so Java rejects the pair with a compile-time name-clash error.
cards.misconception: Different List type arguments distinguish overloads after compilation.

cards.statement: The objects from `new ArrayList<String>()` and `new ArrayList<Integer>()` share a run-time class.
cards.explanation: Both constructions create ArrayList objects. Their generic type arguments do not produce separate run-time classes.

cards.statement: A static method in `class Box<T>` uses the class's `T` as its return type.
cards.explanation: Java rejects a static method's reference to its class's T. The class's type parameter is unavailable in a static context.
cards.misconception: Static methods have access to their class's type parameter.

cards.statement: For a `List<? extends Number> xs`, `xs.add(null)` compiles.
cards.explanation: The wildcard captures an unknown Number subtype. The null type is compatible with that captured reference type.

cards.statement: For a `List<? super Integer> xs`, `xs.add(Integer.valueOf(4))` compiles.
cards.explanation: A lower bound of Integer makes an Integer value valid for add, even though the list's exact element type is unknown.

cards.statement: A reference typed as Map fits a parameter declared as Collection through interface inheritance.
cards.explanation: Map and Collection have separate interface hierarchies. Java rejects passing a Map-typed reference as a Collection argument.
cards.misconception: Map belongs to the Collection inheritance hierarchy.

cards.statement: Calling `put(null, "v")` on a HashMap stores a mapping under the null key.
cards.explanation: HashMap permits the null key, so put can associate it with the value "v".

cards.statement: A HashSet's insertion order determines its specified iteration order.
cards.explanation: HashSet specifies no iteration order; its order may change over time.
cards.misconception: HashSet preserves insertion order during iteration.

cards.statement: In an access-order LinkedHashMap, `get` places an existing entry last in encounter order.
cards.explanation: In access-order mode, LinkedHashMap orders entries from least to most recently accessed; get counts as an access.

cards.statement: Adding through a modifiable reversed() view updates its underlying SequencedCollection.
cards.explanation: An accepted modification through a reversed view updates its underlying collection; reversed() supplies a view rather than an independent copy.

cards.statement: TreeSet.addFirst inserts its argument at the start of the set's encounter order.
cards.explanation: TreeSet.addFirst throws UnsupportedOperationException because comparison determines element positions.
cards.misconception: TreeSet supports explicit first-position insertion through addFirst.

cards.statement: LinkedHashSet.addFirst puts an existing element first in the set's encounter order.
cards.explanation: LinkedHashSet.addFirst relocates an existing element when necessary to make it first.

cards.statement: `List.of("a", null)` throws NullPointerException while creating the list.
cards.explanation: List.of rejects null elements during construction, so this call fails with NullPointerException.

cards.statement: `Set.of("a", "a")` creates a single-element set by merging its duplicate arguments.
cards.explanation: Set.of rejects duplicate elements with IllegalArgumentException.
cards.misconception: Set.of silently merges equal arguments into one element.

cards.statement: A list returned by Collections.unmodifiableList reflects changes made to its backing list.
cards.explanation: Collections.unmodifiableList answers queries through its backing list, so updates made to that list remain visible.

cards.statement: `Arrays.asList("a").add("b")` appends "b" to the returned list.
cards.explanation: Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list. Its add operation throws UnsupportedOperationException.
cards.misconception: The list returned by Arrays.asList grows through add.

cards.statement: The ArrayList API promises ConcurrentModificationException for cross-thread structural changes.
cards.explanation: ArrayList iterators detect concurrent modification on a best-effort basis; ConcurrentModificationException is not guaranteed.
cards.misconception: Fail-fast iteration reliably detects cross-thread structural changes.
